title: Sum Game
statement:
Alice and Bob play a game on the string `num`, which has even length and contains only digits and `'?'` characters. They alternate turns, Alice first: while at least one `'?'` remains, the player to move chooses any `'?'` and replaces it with a digit from `0` to `9`.

When no `'?'` is left the game is over. Bob wins if the digits of the first half of `num` add up to the same total as the digits of the second half; otherwise Alice wins. If `num` has no `'?'` at all, no moves are made and the halves are compared as they are.

Both players play optimally. Return `true` if Alice wins and `false` if Bob wins.
notes:
## Intuition

A brute force would search the whole game tree, but only three things matter: how many `'?'` each half still has and the current difference between the halves. A few strategy facts then give a closed formula.

- If the number of `'?'` is odd, Alice makes the last move. At most one digit would balance the halves, so she picks any other and wins.
- Otherwise Bob can mirror. Whenever Alice fills a `'?'` in one half, Bob answers with the same digit in the other half, cancelling her move. Once one half runs out of marks, the surplus marks sit in a single half and come in pairs: Alice writes `x`, Bob writes `9 - x`, so every pair adds exactly `9`.
- So the half with surplus `k` marks gains exactly `9 * k / 2`. Bob wins only if that precisely closes the gap; any other gap lets Alice push with `0`s or `9`s.

## Approach

1. Walk over `num`, counting `leftMarks` and `rightMarks` and adding the known digits into `leftSum` and `rightSum`.
2. If the total number of marks is odd, return `true`.
3. Otherwise Bob wins exactly when `2 * (leftSum - rightSum) === 9 * (rightMarks - leftMarks)`; return the negation.

## Example 1, step by step

For `"5023"` the halves are `"50"` and `"23"`: `leftSum = 5`, `rightSum = 5`, no marks. The mark count `0` is even, and `2 * (5 - 5) = 0` equals `9 * (0 - 0) = 0`, so Bob wins and the answer is `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the string.
- Space: O(1): four counters.

## Pitfalls

- Marks in different halves cancel each other; only the difference `rightMarks - leftMarks` matters, not the total.
- Each surplus pair adds `9`, not `18`: multiply by 2 on the left side of the test instead of dividing, so no fractions appear.
- A string with no `'?'` is still a valid game: compare the halves directly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `half` | length of each half |
| `leftSum`, `rightSum` | sums of the known digits in each half |
| `leftMarks`, `rightMarks` | number of `'?'` in each half |
| `isLeft` | whether index `i` is in the first half |

narration.2: Each half has num.length / 2 characters; indices below half belong to the first half.
narration.8: Scan every character once to gather the four counters.
narration.9: Note which half index i falls in.
narration.10: A question mark is an open move: count it instead of adding a digit.
narration.12: One more mark in the first half.
narration.14: One more mark in the second half.
narration.17: A known digit in the first half adds to leftSum.
narration.19: A known digit in the second half adds to rightSum.
narration.23: With an odd number of marks Alice moves last and can always break the balance.
narration.26: With an even count, Bob's mirroring makes the surplus half gain exactly 9 per pair; Alice wins unless that closes the gap exactly.
